ChainRungOut.description: One entry in the rendered chain: a real rung, or the trailing HR-fallback marker.
ChainRungOut.title: ChainRungOut

DecisionIn.description:
`POST /requests/{id}/decision` (ADR-0006 §7). `comment` is optional for **both**
outcomes — a server rule, not a UI choice (§7 amended): a mandatory field the server does not
enforce drifts the moment a second client exists.
DecisionIn.title: DecisionIn

DelegateCandidateOut.description:
One `GET /delegate-candidates` row (ADR-0006 §11, screens §4.E). Deliberately three
fields and nothing else — no location, no status, no manager: the picker needs enough to
tell two colleagues apart, never more (ADR-0006 §11: "exposes no PII — a name and a staff
number, to a colleague in the same tenant").
DelegateCandidateOut.title: DelegateCandidateOut

DelegationCreateIn.description:
`POST /delegations` (ADR-0006 §5, §11). `delegator_employee_id` omitted means "for
myself" — the ordinary member flow; supplying a different id needs `delegation.write:ORG`
("for another employee", screens §4.E), checked in `app/api/routes.py` before this reaches
`app/services.create_delegation` at all, so a below-ORG caller's business-rule refusals
(self-delegation, window checks) never leak *anything* about a delegator they are not
authorized to name.
DelegationCreateIn.title: DelegationCreateIn

DelegationCreateOut.description:
`POST /delegations`'s own response — `DelegationOut` plus the one field only a create
response carries (ADR-0006 §11 amended, screens **C4**): how many of the delegator's
currently open steps re-pointed to the delegate in the same transaction. `0` is a normal,
common value (nothing was waiting, or the delegation starts in the future) — the client
omits the "N requests moved" line entirely rather than rendering "0 requests moved".
DelegationCreateOut.title: DelegationCreateOut

DelegationOut.description:
One `GET /delegations` row, and the shape `POST /delegations` and
`POST /delegations/{id}/revoke` both return (ADR-0006 §11, screens §4.E). Both parties carry
a name (§11's "every id is accompanied by a name") but not an `employee_no` — that field
travels only with the person being *identified* (screens **C6**), and a delegation row
identifies nobody in the sense a request's requester does.
DelegationOut.title: DelegationOut

DottedLineManagerOut.description: Shown, never routed (ADR-0006 §2). Absent from the response when there is none.
DottedLineManagerOut.title: DottedLineManagerOut

InboxItemOut.description:
One `GET /inbox` row (ADR-0006 §11, screens §4.A). `request_note` and the requester's
`employee_no` both travel here — the inbox is where triage happens and where confusing two
people has consequences (screens §2.2, §2.9).
InboxItemOut.title: InboxItemOut

RequestDetailOut.description:
`GET /requests/{id}` and the response of `POST .../decision` (ADR-0006 §11). The OWN-scope
read widens to anyone who ever appeared on a step, any outcome — a past decider keeps the
same shape a currently-eligible caller gets, minus the ability to act.
RequestDetailOut.title: RequestDetailOut

RequestListItemOut.description:
One `GET /requests` row (ADR-0006 §11, screens §4.D). No `request_note` — deliberately
(screens §2.9: the requester wrote it, nothing renders it back to them).
RequestListItemOut.title: RequestListItemOut

StepOut.description:
One row of a request's history (ADR-0006 §3, §11) — append-only, so this is the whole
story of how the request got to where it is now.
StepOut.title: StepOut

info.description: The platform's routing engine for who may say yes, who says it when they do not, and how the answer gets back to the product that asked (ADR-0006). Slice 1: the read-only copy of the reporting line (`hierarchy_nodes`) and the resolved chain endpoint. Slice 2: opening and deciding a `hrms.time.regularization` request — routing, delegation applied at open, the inbox, and the product's application-state return leg. No SLA clock yet: every step opens with `due_at = NULL` until slice 4.
info.title: Approval service

get.description:
`core.approval.request.read` — OWN reaches only the caller's own chain; TEAM reaches a
direct report's; LOCATION reaches an employee at one of the caller's locations; ORG reaches
any.

Object-level check runs before either query: `assert_can_touch` is the same chokepoint every
other detail endpoint in the platform uses, and a caller outside scope is refused with 403
before the chain walk ever runs (ADR-0003 §3's negative-authz discipline). TEAM and LOCATION
compare the *subject's* manager and location against the caller — never the caller's own —
so the subject's own hierarchy row is fetched first, ahead of the check, one indexed lookup
the walk needs anyway for the response's `location_code`. A subject the copy has not seen
yet fails TEAM and LOCATION closed (there is nothing to compare against); OWN and ORG are
unaffected, because neither reads the copy to decide.
get.summary: The resolved approval chain for one employee

get.description:
`GET /delegate-candidates` (ADR-0006 §11, screens §4.E): the delegation picker's source.
Gated on `delegation.write` at **any** scope — reachable only by someone who could actually
create a delegation, not a general employee directory (this is why the endpoint exists
instead of widening an HRMS scope, ADR-0006 §11). Excludes the caller and every exited node;
`q` is required and at least two characters **after stripping whitespace**:
`StringConstraints(strip_whitespace=True, min_length=2)` strips before it measures, not
after, so a request whose `q` is all whitespace (`"  "`) or is one real character padded
with whitespace (`"a "`) is a clean 422 here rather than reaching
`selectors.search_delegate_candidates` as an empty or one-character prefix. That distinction
is not cosmetic: `delegation.write` collapses to OWN in the default MEMBER template
(`app/catalogue.py`), so every employee holds it, and a prefix search with no effective floor
is a staff-directory enumeration ("a ".."z ", "0 ".."9 ") any employee could run to
completion in a few dozen requests — well under the gateway's per-minute rate limit. Capped
at `DELEGATE_CANDIDATES_LIMIT` regardless of how many rows match.

schema.title: Response List Delegate Candidates Api V1 Approvals Delegate Candidates Get

get.summary: Delegations I hold (OWN) or every delegation (ORG)

post.description:
`POST /delegations` (ADR-0006 §5, §11). `delegator_employee_id` omitted resolves to the
caller; supplying a *different* id needs ORG (screens §4.E's "for another employee") — a
below-ORG caller doing so is refused here, at the permission boundary, before
`app/services.create_delegation` ever runs, so a business-rule refusal (self-delegation, an
overlap) can never leak anything about a delegator the caller was never authorized to name.
Every other refusal — self-delegation, an end before or in the past, an overlapping active
delegation, a delegate who has left — is `app/services.create_delegation`'s.

`POST /delegations/{id}/revoke` (ADR-0006 §5, §11). `app/services.revoke_delegation` is
where the object-level rule lives: below ORG only the delegator may revoke, a bystander gets
**404**, an already-revoked delegation gets a clean **409** rather than the guard trigger's
raw exception.

get.description:
`GET /inbox` (ADR-0006 §11): pending requests where ADR-0006 §6 makes the caller eligible
— unassigned rows only for a `decide:ORG` holder — excluding the caller's own requests.

A caller with no `subject_ref` is eligible for nothing (§6 rule 2: "a membership with no
employee link can decide nothing, including unassigned steps") — an empty page, not a 403,
the same "let the server's own filtering be the gate" pattern screens §2.4 specifies for this
endpoint.
get.summary: Pending requests the caller may decide

get.description:
`GET /requests` (ADR-0006 §11): OWN = `requester_employee_id = sref`; TEAM = raised by a
direct report; LOCATION = raised by anyone at one of the caller's locations; ORG = every
request — all via `ctx.apply()` in `selectors.requests_stmt`. No `request_note` (screens
§2.9 — nothing renders the requester's own text back to them); `application_state` travels
here, deliberately (C8).

`?requester=me` is the "My requests" screen's own filter, layered on top of scope rather than
a replacement for it: scope answers "may this caller see this row", not "is this caller's
own" — a TEAM, LOCATION or ORG reader legitimately sees other people's requests through this
same endpoint (the HR/ORG "all requests" view screens also describe), so without this filter
an ORG-scoped caller asking for "my requests" would be shown the entire organization's. The
server resolves "me" from `ctx.subject_ref`, never a client-supplied id — `Literal["me"]` is
the whole of the accepted vocabulary, so there is no `requester=<uuid>` shape to accept or
reject in application code at all; anything else fails FastAPI's own query validation before
this function runs (422), which is the boundary validation CLAUDE.md asks for rather than a
second, hand-rolled check here.
get.summary: Requests I raised (OWN) or every request (ORG)

get.description:
`GET /requests/{id}` (ADR-0006 §11, amended): OWN reaches the requester, **or anyone who
appears on a step of this request, any outcome** — a past decider, a past delegate, anyone
escalated past, keeps full read access to what they took part in. ORG reaches any. A caller
who cannot see the request gets **404, not 403** (ADR-0006 §11: "so that request ids cannot
be probed"), and a wrong-tenant id is indistinguishable from one that never existed.

post.description:
`POST /requests/{id}/decision` (ADR-0006 §7). `require("core.approval.request.decide")`
is only the first gate; `app/services.decide_request` re-checks ADR-0006 §6 under the
request row's lock and is what actually decides who may act — **403** not eligible, **409**
already decided (with the recorded outcome, via the conflict message).
post.summary: Approve or reject a pending request

get.description:
How far behind the relay is. **Alert on `oldest_seconds`.**

A stalled relay is the platform's quietest failure. It selects, finds nothing,
logs nothing, sleeps, and loops — `attempts` never increments and `last_error`
stays null, so the process looks healthy indefinitely while the outbox grows
without bound and every consumer downstream starves.

Deliberately **not** part of readiness. A backlog is not a reason to take the
service out of rotation: refusing traffic would stop new events being written
without helping drain the ones already queued, which makes the incident worse.
This is a metric to alert on, not a health state.

Counted through the outbox engine, not the application one. The app role is
NOBYPASSRLS and this request binds no tenant, so through it `pending` would be
zero whatever the table holds — the probe that exists to expose the stall would
be wired to the same blind spot that causes it.
get.summary: Outbox depth and age — scrape this

get.description:
Route traffic on this; restart on /health.

Conflating the two restarts a healthy process that is merely waiting on a
dependency.

Only the dependencies a service actually declares are checked. A gateway owns no
tables, so asking it for a database is asking a question whose answer means nothing
— and a readiness probe that reports on something the service does not use is worse
than no probe, because it will eventually fail for a reason nobody can act on.
